title: AI observability: tracing a chain, logging prompts, drift
story:
A request now passes through several model calls, retrievals and tool invocations. When the final answer is wrong there is no stack trace, because nothing threw — every step returned something plausible, and the wrongness is distributed across a chain of individually reasonable outputs.

The structure of the answer is the one from the observability lesson, and it transfers directly. The tracing design states its goals as low overhead, application-level transparency, and ubiquitous deployment on a very large scale system, carrying a trace context associated with a thread that is tracked across asynchronous callbacks and remote calls, with traces formally modelled as trees. A chain of model calls is a tree of exactly that shape. Instrument the shared client rather than each application, propagate context across every call, and you get the causal structure for free.

What is different is what has to be inside each span, and the difference is the whole lesson. For an ordinary service, knowing that a call took ninety milliseconds and returned a success code is usually enough. For a model call it is nearly useless — every step succeeded, that is the problem. The evidence you need is the content: the exact prompt after templating, the retrieved passages that went into it, the raw output before parsing, the tool arguments and what the tool returned. The intermediate text is the only record of where the reasoning went wrong.

That requirement collides with two things ordinary request logging does not have to face. It is expensive, because the state associated with one call is neither small nor fixed — the per-request cache is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically over the life of that request, and the text you are storing grows the same way. And it is the user's content plus the model's raw output, which makes it a retention and privacy problem rather than a volume problem. So you cannot simply log everything forever, and the sampling that saved the general case saves you here too — the finding being that a sample of one in thousands provides sufficient information for many common uses, with restricted instrumentation and sampling both named as central to that design's success.

Drift is the piece with no analogue in ordinary observability. A service that is not deployed does not change. A model-backed system changes because its inputs change, because a provider updated something underneath you, or because the corpus behind retrieval was edited. So the monitoring has to include the inputs and the outputs as distributions rather than only the requests as events — and the measurement that catches it is a fixed set of cases run on a schedule against production, which is the evaluation lesson operating continuously rather than at release.

problem.name: Tracing a model chain
problem.shape: A wrong answer emerges from a chain in which every individual step succeeded and returned something plausible.
tell: an answer is wrong and no component reported an error
debugging means re-running by hand and hoping it reproduces
nobody can retrieve the exact prompt that produced a given output

problem.move: Trace the chain as a tree by propagating context through every call, and record the content at each span — the templated prompt, the retrieved passages, the raw output, the tool arguments and results. Sample deliberately, set retention on the basis that this is user content, and run a fixed set of cases against production on a schedule to catch drift.
problem.invariant: For an ordinary service the metadata suffices; for a model call the content is the evidence, because every step succeeded and the failure is in what was said rather than in whether it returned.
problem.breaks: The records that make debugging possible are the user's content and the model's raw output, so the retention that would make them useful is the retention that makes them a liability. That tension has no technical resolution — it is a policy decision about how long you keep other people's text.

cost.time: serialisation of large text payloads on the hot path, which is why sampling matters more here than for ordinary tracing
cost.space: orders of magnitude more per span than metadata, and growing with the length of what was generated
cost.beats: metadata-only tracing, which tells you every step succeeded — which you already knew — and re-running by hand, which does not reproduce

worked.problem: What do you need to record to debug a wrong answer from a chain of model calls?
worked.reasoning:
The content at every step, not the metadata — because the metadata will tell you that everything worked, which is already established by the fact that you got an answer at all.

Start with what makes this different. In an ordinary service, a failure announces itself: something threw, returned an error code, or timed out, and the trace showing which span failed is most of the diagnosis. In a chain of model calls there is no such signal. Every call returned successfully, within its latency budget, with well-formed output. The answer is wrong anyway, and the wrongness is somewhere in what was said rather than in whether anything returned.

So the span needs the text. Specifically: the exact prompt after templating, because the bug is frequently in the template rather than the model and the rendered prompt is the only place that shows. The retrieved passages that went into it, because the retrieval lesson establishes that this is the most likely failure point and a retriever fails by returning plausible irrelevant material. The raw model output before any parsing, because a parsing layer that silently coerces malformed output turns a visible failure into an invisible one. And the tool arguments and returns, because an agent that called the right tool with the wrong arguments looks identical from outside to one that called the wrong tool.

The structure to put that in is the ordinary one. A chain is a tree, which is exactly how traces are formally modelled, and you get it by propagating a context through every call — with application-level transparency achieved by instrumenting the shared client rather than each application, which is what made the general design work and works here for the same reason.

Then the two constraints that make this harder than ordinary tracing. It is large: the state associated with one call is neither small nor fixed, since the per-request cache is huge and grows and shrinks dynamically, and the text grows the same way. And it is user content plus raw model output, which is a privacy and retention question rather than a storage one. Those pull in opposite directions — the retention that makes the records useful is the retention that makes them a liability — and there is no technical resolution, only a policy decision.

Sampling is the lever, and the same finding applies: one request in thousands provides sufficient information for many common uses, with restricted instrumentation and sampling both named as central to the design's success. I would add one modification for this setting: sample failures and low-confidence outputs at a much higher rate than successes, because unlike ordinary latency debugging you usually know which requests were bad.

And the thing I would raise unprompted is drift, because it has no analogue. A service that is not deployed does not change; a model-backed system changes when its inputs change, when a provider updates something underneath you, or when the corpus behind retrieval is edited. So monitoring has to treat inputs and outputs as distributions rather than as events, and the detector is a fixed set of cases run against production on a schedule — the evaluation lesson operating continuously rather than at release.

problem.practice: Take a wrong answer your system produced and try to retrieve the exact prompt that caused it. If you cannot, that is the gap. Then check what your parsing layer does with malformed model output — whether it raises or quietly coerces.

beats.broke: A request passes through several model calls, retrievals and tool invocations, and when the final answer is wrong there is no stack trace — every step returned something plausible.
beats.fix: Trace the chain as a tree the way any distributed request is traced, and record the actual inputs and outputs at every step, because the intermediate text is the only evidence of where the reasoning went wrong.
beats.cost: Those intermediate records are the user's content and the model's raw output, so the thing that makes debugging possible is also a retention, privacy and cost problem that ordinary request logging does not have.
